newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombia's Ecopetrol says no renegotiation.
newsitem.headline: Colombia's Ecopetrol says no renegotiation.

text.p: Colombia's state-run oil company Ecopetrol will not renegotiate any association contracts with private sector producers, the head of the company said in a press release Monday.

"The seriousness and long term stability of our terms has gained Ecopetrol wide recognition within the international oil industry. Within that framework we do not contemplate any revision of association contracts," Antonio Jose Urdinola said.

Ecopetrol currently has 94 association contracts with 63 private sector companies from 17 countries, including Colombia. In Monday's statement the company said it would sign 11 more association contracts in the coming weeks.
Britain's British Petroleum Co Plc is Colombia's biggest single investor and has been pushing hard for sweeter contract terms on the Piedemonte oil field it operates in the eastern plains region.

Three hydrocarbon formations have been discovered in the area so far but BP says potential profit margins on the field, expected to come onstream before the turn of the millennium, are not sufficient.

Under the terms of the so-called sliding scale contract BP will pay an increasingly larger slice of the profits to Ecopetrol as output rises, topping out at about a 70 percent share for the Colombian state oil company.

Negotiations are still under way between BP and Ecopetrol, although the short-term profitability of the field was boosted when the Colombian government redefined the terms of the contract earlier this year.

But in what appeared to be an implicit reference to BP and other companies which may be looking to follow the British multinational's lead in pressing for changes in contract conditions, Urdinola said: "The changes made to the terms of the model association contract have been exclusively for new contracts, and in no case, have they been applied to existing contracts."
BP sources say talks with Ecopetrol about the Piedemonte field are at an "advanced stage".

They are centering around Colombia's suggestion that BP could hand back most of the hitherto unexplored area of the field and be reawarded part of it under a so-called Factor R contract, which takes into account investments and difficult drilling conditions to ensure the operator sufficient profit margins.
